title: Making Sense of Morphemes: Prioritize Progressions
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos takes up a debate in the SPELL-Talk community about when to introduce morphology in beginning reading, and argues for a graded progression. Drawing on Jan Wasowicz, David Share and Alex Quigley, she holds that early encoding and decoding should start with simple, concrete, transparent monomorphemic words such as cat and bag. Inflectional morphemes follow once the alphabetic principle is secure, with derivational morphology building over many years. She points to the order in which children acquire morphemes in spoken language as support for this sequence and notes that read-alouds and teachable moments still expose children to multimorphemic words. The orchestra metaphor of adding instruments gradually frames her case that instruction should respect cognitive load rather than teach everything at once. She closes with questions teachers can use to decide which morphemes to teach, and how.
points: Early reading instruction should begin with monomorphemic, concrete and transparent words so beginners can practice encoding and decoding without extra complexity.
Children's spoken-language acquisition of morphemes follows a predictable order, which the author uses as a template for sequencing instruction.
Incidental exposure to morphemes in read-alouds and writing is distinguished from deliberate teaching, so teachers should know which one they are doing.
Wasowicz's orchestra metaphor treats multi-component literacy as adding sections gradually, not everything at once.
The closing questions give teachers a practical check on which morphemes, how, and with what cognitive load.
quotes: The point is that each of these three morphemes has a time and place within a program’s scope and sequence, in addition to the incidental occurrences (teachable moments) within the course of a day’s interactions between teacher and students, always bound by instructional constraints related to cognitive load.
The sticking point comes from those who believe that prioritizing these monomorphemic words during beginning reading instruction robs students of the opportunity to develop morphological awareness.
Their simplicity, concreteness, and phonological/orthographic transparency make them ideal candidates for the beginning reading instruction David Share describes.

But at the very beginning, children generally do not have the reading skill and stamina to blend across a multisyllabic word even if it is part of their lexicon and has a structure that is orthographically transparent.

The point is that at the very beginning—when students are learning to segment sounds to write (encode) and to blend sounds to read (decode)—we do not burden them unnecessarily with the complexity of juggling too many units of language, though we take advantage of teachable moments to introduce where morphemes appear in words and how they can have stable spellings but variable pronunciations.

Multi-component literacy instruction and instructional simultaneity does not mean ‘everything, everywhere all at once.’ It’s more like preparing an orchestra: at first, instruction works with a smaller section of instruments (e.g., phonology, orthography, and meaning to read and spell words), while other sections (e.g., morphology, syntax, and higher-order language skills) are being tuned separately.
Are we careful to distinguish between explicit instruction and incidental learning? Are we aware of methods that simplify any inherent complexity?
